desc: THIS NODE EXISTS TO STOP ONE SPECIFIC INFERENCE. The Disclosure Project produced two things a month apart: a Briefing Document dated April 2001 printing 68 testimonies, and a press conference on 9 May 2001 at which 20 of the 69 people interviewed for the accompanying book spoke. They are not the same roster and no opened source lists the 20. The ARV build hit this in September 2026 with Mark McCandlish, whose testimony is dated December 2000 and whom no opened record places at the podium, and the problem is structural rather than particular to him: forty-nine interviewees did not speak and nobody has published which forty-nine. Five people are placed at the podium by sources opened on 19 September 2026: John Callahan and Clifford Stone, Major George A. Filer III, Daniel Sheehan and Alfred L. Webre. Two of those attestations are independent of the organiser, because Klass names Callahan and Filer from the coverage and places Stone there by way of Fox News Channel footage. The date, venue and scale are solid, confirmed the same day by ABC News and within weeks by a hostile contemporaneous newsletter. The webcast audience figures that circulate in the literature come from the Project's own publicity and are not carried here.

dossier.narrative:
The event is documented. ABC News reported it the same day under the headline 'Group Calls for Disclosure of UFO Info', recording that Steven Greer organised the programme at the National Press Club and that about twenty people spoke. Philip Klass, hostile and writing within weeks, gives the same date, the same venue and the same count, and states the objective as prompting a congressional hearing. Two sources of opposite disposition agreeing on date, venue and count is as solid as this subject gets.

What is not documented is who stood there. Klass records that Greer's book contains transcripts of interviews with sixty-nine witnesses, of whom twenty spoke briefly at the press conference. The board has been able to place five of those twenty by an opened source: John Callahan, who described the JAL incident; Clifford Stone, shown there by Fox News Channel; and three others. **Nothing opened by this board places Karl Wolfe, Donna Hare, Robert Jacobs, Larry Warren, Don Phillips or Mark McCandlish at this podium**, and all six are routinely said to have spoken there.

That gap is not a failure of research effort. The Internet Archive is unreachable from this session, both WorldCat records returned 403, and no C-SPAN record of the event exists. The roster may simply not survive in any open form, and the board should say that rather than repeat an assumption.

One limitation on the best hostile source, recorded because it cuts both ways: Klass did not attend. Greer had refused him admission to a comparable event in 1997. That limits his account of what was said at the podium; it does not limit the records he obtained himself, which is where his value on this board lies.
openQuestions: THE PODIUM ROSTER ITSELF. Which twenty of the sixty-nine spoke. The Internet Archive was unreachable, both WorldCat records returned HTTP 403, and no C-SPAN record of the event exists. This is the highest-value single gap in the cluster.
Whether any complete recording of the event survives in an openable form.
Whether the National Press Club's own records name the speakers.
dossier.whatItIs: The Disclosure Project press conference at the National Press Club in Washington DC on 9 May 2001, at which about twenty of the project's sixty-nine interviewees spoke briefly and called for congressional hearings with subpoena power and amnesty for witnesses. It is a distinct object from the April 2001 Briefing Document and it carries a different and much smaller evidentiary weight, which is the entire reason it has its own node.
dossier.whyImplicated: Because almost everything attributed to it is unverifiable, and saying so precisely is worth a node. This press conference is the single most-cited event in modern disclosure advocacy, and the board can place exactly five people at its podium from opened sources. Treating the event and the document as one object, which the literature routinely does, silently upgrades a printed testimony into a public appearance. This node exists to stop that.
